title: Spiritual Gifts and Speaking in Tongues
lead: The abilities the New Testament says the Holy Spirit gives to believers for the good of the church: prophecy, healing, teaching, leading, giving, speaking in tongues and their interpretation, and more (1 Corinthians 12–14; Romans 12:6–8). Speaking in tongues appears first at Pentecost (Acts 2:4), and Christians still differ over what it was and whether such gifts continue today.

sections.h: Tongues in Acts and in Corinth
sections.b: At Pentecost the believers speak in other languages that visitors from many nations understand (Acts 2:4–11). Tongues return when the Spirit comes on Gentiles at Caesarea and on John's disciples at Ephesus (Acts 10:46; Acts 19:6). In Corinth, Paul describes tongues as speech to God that no one understands without an interpreter (1 Corinthians 14:2, 27–28). Readers ask whether these are the same gift: known human languages (xenolalia), or speech in no known language (glossolalia), or both.

Pentecostal and charismatic Christians teach that all the gifts continue, and classical Pentecostals hold that speaking in tongues is the first outward sign of being baptized in the Spirit. Cessationists, many of them Reformed or dispensational, hold that sign gifts such as tongues and prophecy ended with the apostles. Many Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist Christians take a middle view: the Spirit may give any gift, but no gift is required as proof of the Spirit.
